title: Conway's Game of Life
description: Compute the next generation of a 2D grid. Each cell's fate depends on its 8 neighbors: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbors survives; a dead cell with exactly 3 becomes alive. Write to a fresh grid — never mutate while iterating, or later cells will read updated state.

notes: Always write to a separate output grid. In-place mutation corrupts the neighbor counts of cells you have not visited yet.
Live survives on 2 or 3 neighbors; dead births on EXACTLY 3. Anything else is death (under/overpopulation).
Skip dr=dc=0 (the cell itself) when summing the 8 neighbors, and bounds-check every (nr, nc).

questions.q: Why use a separate output grid instead of updating in place?
options: Updates would change neighbor counts read by later cells
Conway specified it in the rules

questions.q: A dead cell becomes alive when its live-neighbor count is...
A live cell with 4 live neighbors...
options: Triggers a birth in an adjacent dead cell

questions.q: How many neighbors does an interior cell have?

exercises.prompt: Fill in nextGen so the blinker [[0,0,0],[1,1,1],[0,0,0]] becomes a vertical bar.

L3.prompt: Implement nextGen(grid) and log JSON for: gen1 and gen2 of a 4x4 block (still life), then gen1 and gen2 of a 3x3 blinker.
hints: Sum the 8 neighbors with bounds checks; skip (0,0).
Branch on the current cell's state — alive uses {2,3}, dead uses {3}.
Write into a fresh grid so in-flight updates do not contaminate neighbor counts.
